article.title: How to reduce no-shows without losing good clients

sections.text: Most no-shows come from clients who forgot, or who could not reach you to move the time, not from clients who do not care. By the end of this edition you will have a two-reminder routine you can switch on this week, the exact words to use, and a simple way to see whether it is working.

sections.heading: Where no-shows come from
sections.text: When you ask owners why clients miss appointments, the first answer is usually that some people are just unreliable. Look closer at your own list and a different picture shows up. Most missed appointments were booked weeks ago, often by phone, and the client never got anything in writing. Some clients meant to cancel but your line was busy, the form was hard to find, or it felt awkward to call. A smaller group double-booked themselves with work or family. Only a small share of no-shows are people who simply did not care. That matters, because the first three groups respond to a better routine, and only the last one needs a policy. Before you change anything, pull last month's numbers: how many appointments you had, how many were missed without notice, and how many were cancelled with less than a day's warning. Write them down, because you will compare against them in four weeks. If you do not track this today, start with a tally on paper at the front desk for two weeks. Across the businesses that book through our app, [share of missed appointments that had no written confirmation, from your own booking data] of missed appointments had no written confirmation at all.

sections.heading: The two-reminder routine
sections.text: One reminder is better than none, but two reminders at the right moments do most of the work. Set it up in three steps. 1. Send the first reminder when the booking is made, so the client has the date, time, place and a way to change it in writing from day one. 2. Send the second reminder before the appointment, early enough that a cancelled slot can still be filled. For most salon and studio services, a day before works well. For longer clinic appointments, or services that need preparation, two or three days before gives you time to rebook. 3. Decide who watches the replies, and when, so a reschedule request never waits until after the slot has passed. Each reminder should do one job: get a reply. Ask the client to confirm or to pick a new time, and make both options one tap or one short word. A reminder that only informs is easy to ignore; a reminder that asks a question gets answered. Keep the text short enough to read on a lock screen, and put your business name in the first few words, so the client knows who it is from before they open it. Most booking tools can send both reminders on their own once you set the timing.

sections.heading: What to say in each reminder
sections.text: Here is a pattern that works for the booking reminder: your business name, the service, the day and time, and one line that says how to change it. For example, a salon might send: [your business name]: you are booked for a cut and colour on Thursday at 2pm. Need a different time? Reply CHANGE and we will sort it. For the second reminder, add the question: [your business name]: see you tomorrow at 2pm for your cut and colour. Reply YES to confirm or CHANGE to pick a new time. Avoid three things. Do not open with a long greeting, because the preview cuts off before the time. Do not mention fees in the first reminder; it reads as a threat to a client who has done nothing wrong. And do not send the second reminder in the evening if your front desk only answers in the morning, because a CHANGE reply that sits overnight is a slot you cannot refill. If you already have a deposit or cancellation policy, link to it once, in plain words, in the booking reminder. Our guide to reminder wording has more templates you can copy for different services. Read each one out loud before you switch it on: if it sounds like a bank, rewrite it in the way your front desk talks.

sections.heading: How to know it is working
sections.text: Give the routine four weeks before you judge it, so one quiet week or one busy holiday does not mislead you. Then compare three numbers against the ones you wrote down at the start: missed appointments without notice, late cancellations, and replies to the second reminder. If missed appointments fell but late cancellations rose, the routine is working: clients who used to vanish are now telling you, and a late cancellation is a slot you can still try to fill. If replies are low, shorten the second reminder and move the question to the first line. If nothing changed, look at timing: a reminder that arrives after the client has already made other plans is too late. Change one thing at a time, and give each change two weeks, so you know which one moved the number. Share the result with your team, because the people at the front desk are the ones who will keep the routine alive on a busy day. One proof point to add here before you publish: [a customer result you have written permission to share: their no-show rate before and after two reminders]. If you do not have one yet, leave this paragraph out rather than guess.

Want the full set of tactics, with the reminder templates in one place? Read the guide: https://www.example.com/blog/reduce-no-shows/. Next edition, on December 3: what a fair cancellation fee looks like.
